description: Nobody calls a trigger — the database fires it when data changes. BEFORE vs AFTER, row vs statement, :NEW and :OLD, and when triggers are brilliant vs when they're a trap.

screens.body: Everything so far was logic someone CALLS. Triggers flip that: nobody calls a trigger — the database fires it automatically when data changes. Insert a row? The trigger runs. Update a price? The trigger runs. They're event-driven: the event is a data change, and the trigger is the response. Set it and forget it — the database remembers.

options: You call it like a procedure
The database fires it when data changes
check.question: What makes a trigger run?

screens.heading: Events, not calls
screens.keyPoint: Triggers fire automatically on data changes — never called directly.

screens.body: A trigger has three parts: WHEN it fires (BEFORE or AFTER the change), WHAT fires it (INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE), and WHERE (on which table). BEFORE runs before the change hits the table — good for validating or fixing data. AFTER runs once the change is in — good for logging what happened. Timing + event + table: that's the whole anatomy.

options: BEFORE validates/fixes data; AFTER logs what happened
BEFORE is faster; AFTER is slower
check.question: BEFORE vs AFTER?

screens.heading: The anatomy: timing + event + table

screens.body: Triggers come in two granularities. Row-level (FOR EACH ROW) fires once PER ROW — and gives you :NEW (the row's new values) and :OLD (its old values). Statement-level fires ONCE per statement, no matter how many rows changed — and gets no :NEW/:OLD. Updating 100 rows? Row-level fires 100 times; statement-level fires once.

options: Row-level fires per row with :NEW/:OLD; statement-level fires once
check.question: Row-level vs statement-level?

screens.heading: Row vs statement: how often it fires

screens.body: :NEW and :OLD are snapshots of the row. In an INSERT, :NEW is the incoming row (:OLD doesn't exist — there was no 'before'). In a DELETE, :OLD is the departing row. In an UPDATE, you get both — perfect for comparisons like 'did the price actually change?' or audit logs recording old → new.

options: The row's values after the change
The user who made the change
check.question: In a trigger, :NEW is…

code.snippet:
CREATE TRIGGER audit_price
AFTER UPDATE OF price ON products
FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  INSERT INTO price_log(product_id, old_price, new_price)
  VALUES (:OLD.id, :OLD.price, :NEW.price);
END;

screens.heading: :NEW and :OLD: before/after snapshots

screens.body: Triggers shine for rules no app should be allowed to skip. Audit logging: who changed what, when — automatically. Auto-maintained columns: updated_at timestamps without trusting every app to set them. Data guardrails: reject negative prices or impossible dates at the database level, where no buggy client can dodge them.

options: Enforcing rules no app can bypass, like audit logs
check.question: A genuinely good use for a trigger:

screens.heading: Good uses: the unskippable rules
screens.keyPoint: Audit logs, auto timestamps, guardrails — things that must ALWAYS happen.

screens.body: The dark side: triggers are invisible. Someone updates a row and three triggers fire, updating other tables, which fire more triggers — a cascade nobody can see by reading the app code. Business logic hidden in triggers becomes spaghetti that's brutal to debug. Rule of thumb: triggers for guardrails and logging, NOT for core business logic that belongs in named, callable, testable procedures.

options: Business logic hidden where nobody can see it
They use too much disk space
check.question: Why do experienced devs get nervous about triggers?

screens.heading: Bad uses: invisible spaghetti
screens.keyPoint: Hidden cascading triggers are a debugging nightmare — keep business logic visible.

screens.body: Triggers aren't permanent. ALTER TRIGGER my_trigger DISABLE turns it off without deleting it (handy for bulk loads); ENABLE turns it back on. DROP TRIGGER deletes it for good. And you can check which triggers exist and whether they're enabled by querying the data dictionary — metadata to the rescue again.

check.question: How do you temporarily switch a trigger off?

code.snippet:
ALTER TRIGGER check_price DISABLE;  -- off, but kept
ALTER TRIGGER check_price ENABLE;   -- back on
DROP TRIGGER check_price;           -- gone for good

screens.heading: Managing triggers: on, off, gone
screens.keyPoint: DISABLE pauses, ENABLE resumes, DROP deletes.
